plan.contextChunk: This figure stacks five drawings of the same fixed string. At the top a horizontal line runs between two black endpoint dots, each labeled "Node", with a double-headed dimension arrow above it labeled L. Beneath come four standing-wave patterns on lines of that same length, labeled at the left n = 1, n = 2, n = 3, and n = 4. Each is a dark blue curve with a pale mirror-image curve, the two outlining the envelope the string sweeps, ends pinned and interior crossing points rising from none to three. Two expressions sit to the right of each: 1/2 lambda_1 = L and lambda_1 = 2/1 L, then lambda_2 = L and lambda_2 = 2/2 L, then 3/2 lambda_3 = L and lambda_3 = 2/3 L, then 4/2 lambda_4 = L and lambda_4 = 2/4 L. A general statement closes the lower right, lambda_n = 2/n L for n = 1, 2, 3, and so on. Holding one length fixed while packing in more half-wavelengths shows how the pinned ends restrict which wavelengths fit. The sequence introduces the normal modes of a string fixed at both ends.

interactionPlan.concept: A string fixed at both ends can vibrate only in normal modes where an integer number of half-wavelengths fits exactly into the string length L.

interactions.label: Mode number
interactions.teaches: Each higher mode fits one additional half-wavelength into the same fixed length, creating one more lobe and one more interior node pattern.

interactions.label: Animate selected mode
interactions.teaches: Nodes remain motionless while antinodes move with maximum amplitude, so the envelope curves mark the extremes of the string's oscillation.

interactions.label: String length L
interactions.teaches: For a fixed mode number, changing L stretches or contracts the allowed wavelength in direct proportion according to lambda_n = 2L/n.

demo_steps.narration: In the first normal mode, the fixed endpoints are nodes and the string contains exactly one half-wavelength. The equation reads 1/2 lambda_1 = L, so lambda_1 = 2L.

demo_steps.title: Add another half-wavelength
demo_steps.narration: In the second mode, two half-wavelengths fit into the same length L. The midpoint becomes an interior node, and the allowed wavelength is lambda_2 = L.

demo_steps.title: Higher modes pack more lobes into L
demo_steps.narration: For n = 3 and n = 4, three or four half-wavelengths fit between the pinned ends. More nodes appear because the wave must still be zero at every fixed point.

demo_steps.title: Stretch the string
demo_steps.narration: With the mode number held fixed, increasing L stretches every lobe and increases the wavelength. The number of half-wavelengths does not change; their size changes.

interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean white background and a horizontal layout matching the textbook figure. Put the fixed reference string and L dimension arrow across the top. Below it, show the selected standing-wave mode prominently; optionally include faint stacked thumbnails for the other modes so the learner still senses the original sequence. Draw the active phase curve in medium/dark blue and the opposite phase or envelope in pale blue. Endpoint nodes should be black dots that never move; interior nodes should appear at equal spacing for n > 1. Place equations to the right of the wave, updating them for the selected mode: 1/2 lambda_1 = L and lambda_1 = 2L, lambda_2 = L and lambda_2 = L, 3/2 lambda_3 = L and lambda_3 = 2L/3, or 4/2 lambda_4 = L and lambda_4 = L/2. Keep the general formula lambda_n = 2L/n visible near the bottom right.

- Button/state for mode number: the learner steps through n = 1, 2, 3, and 4, the standing-wave shape, interior nodes, and wavelength equation update, making clear that exactly n half-wavelengths must fit inside length L.
- Animation for the selected mode: the learner presses play for any mode, the string oscillates between the two envelope curves while endpoint and interior nodes stay fixed, making clear the difference between nodes and antinodes.
- Slider for string length L: the learner drags the endpoint separation, the displayed wavelength for the selected mode stretches or contracts with the string, making clear the relationship lambda_n = 2L/n.

authoredContext:
The lab setup shows a string attached to a string vibrator, which oscillates the string with an adjustable frequency f. The other end of the string passes over a frictionless pulley and is tied to a hanging mass. The magnitude of the tension in the string is equal to the weight of the hanging mass. The string has a constant linear density (mass per length) μ and the speed at which a wave travels down the string equals v=FTμ=mgμ another section. The symmetrical boundary conditions (a node at each end) dictate the possible frequencies that can excite standing waves. Starting from a frequency of zero and slowly increasing the frequency, the first mode n=1 appears as shown in the figure. The first mode, also called the fundamental mode or the first harmonic, shows half of a wavelength has formed, so the wavelength is equal to twice the length between the nodes λ1=2L. The fundamental frequency, or first harmonic frequency, that drives this mode is

The standing wave patterns that are possible for a string, the first four of which are shown in the figure, are known as the normal modes, with frequencies known as the normal frequencies. In summary, the first frequency to produce a normal mode is called the fundamental frequency (or first harmonic). Any frequencies above the fundamental frequency are overtones. The second frequency of the n=2 normal mode of the string is the first overtone (or second harmonic). The frequency of the n=3 normal mode is the second overtone (or third harmonic) and so on.

where the speed of the wave is v=FTμ. Keeping the tension constant and increasing the frequency leads to the second harmonic or the n=2 mode. This mode is a full wavelength λ2=L and the frequency is twice the fundamental frequency:

Standing waves created on a string of length L. A node occurs at each end of the string. The nodes are boundary conditions that limit the possible frequencies that excite standing waves. (Note that the amplitudes of the oscillations have been kept constant for visualization. The standing wave patterns possible on the string are known as the normal modes. Conducting this experiment in the lab would result in a decrease in amplitude as the frequency increases.)

Four figures of a string of length L are shown. Each has two waves. The first one has 1 node. It is labeled half lambda 1 = L, lambda 1 = 2 by 1 times L. The second figure has 2 nodes. It is labeled lambda 2 = L, lambda 2 = 2 by 2 times L. The third figure has three nodes. It is labeled 3 by 2 times lambda 3 = L, lambda 3 = 2 by 3 times L. The fourth figure has 4 nodes. It is labeled 4 by 2 times lambda 4 = L, lambda 4 = 2 by 4 times L. There is a derived formula at the bottom, lambda n equal to 2 by n times L for n = 1, 2, 3 and so on.

The next two modes, or the third and fourth harmonics, have wavelengths of λ3=23L and λ4=24L, driven by frequencies of f3=3v2L=3f1 and f4=4v2L=4f1. All frequencies above the frequency f1 are known as the overtones. The equations for the wavelength and the frequency can be summarized as:

discrepancies: The generated figure highlights the n = 1 row with a pale blue background, bold labels, and darker strokes while fading the other modes; the source shows all four modes uniformly with no selected state in the default static view.
Interior node dots are added at the crossings for n = 2, 3, and 4, but the source only marks the endpoints of each string row with black dots.
The right-hand wavelength equations for n = 1 and n = 2 are simplified to λ₁ = 2L and λ₂ = L rather than preserving the source's pattern λ₁ = 2/1 L and λ₂ = 2/2 L.
The bottom formula is rendered with compact Unicode superscript/subscript fraction styling rather than the clearer stacked fraction used in the source, making the pattern less visually faithful.
The generated rows use opacity changes and white-backed equation labels that are not present in the source and slightly alter the clean textbook appearance.
evaluation.notes: The normal-mode structure, endpoint nodes, wavelength relationships, and overall layout are recognizable, but the default selected-row styling, added interior node dots, and simplified equations reduce fidelity to the source.
action_items: Make the default static view match the source by removing the active-row highlight and rendering all four modes with equal opacity, stroke weight, and label weight.
Remove the interior black node dots from the wave rows, or hide them unless an explanatory interaction explicitly enables node markers.
Change the right-side equations to match the source exactly: λ₁ = 2/1 L and λ₂ = 2/2 L rather than simplified equivalents.
Use clearer math-style fraction formatting for the bottom λₙ = 2/n L formula so it visually matches the textbook notation more closely.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interactivity are solid, but the cited issues are concrete rendering and labeling fidelity problems—highlight styling, extra node dots, and equation formatting—that the generator can fix without changing the plan.
